content.title: About
content.content: Cuban bread is a traditional white loaf made from wheat flour, yeast, water, and salt. After baking it is often toasted until golden and crisp, creating a fragrant, crunchy product that is served for breakfast, in sandwiches, or as a side to soups.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cuban bread is known for its soft interior and slightly sweet flavor thanks to a small amount of sugar in the dough.
It is traditionally baked in long loaves that are later sliced and toasted.
In Cuba the bread is commonly served with butter, cheese, ham, or avocado, creating the popular "Cubano" sandwich.
Toasting enhances caramelization, giving the crust a crunch while the crumb stays tender.
Some regions add a little milk to the dough, resulting in an even softer texture.

items.title: Source of carbohydrates
items.content: The bread provides a quick source of energy through easily digestible carbs.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Fermentation by yeast produces B1, B2, and B3 vitamins, important for metabolism.

items.title: Provides dietary fiber
items.content: Although not whole‑grain, Cuban bread still contains a modest amount of fiber that supports digestion.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: It supplies iron, magnesium, and phosphorus, which are essential for blood and bone health.

items.title: Versatile pairing
items.content: Toasted Cuban bread pairs well with proteins and vegetables, helping to create a balanced meal.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: The bread contains gluten and is unsuitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: White bread can cause a rapid rise in blood sugar, which may be problematic for diabetics.

items.title: Salt content
items.content: Traditional recipes may contain a fair amount of salt; those monitoring sodium should limit portions.

items.title: Wheat allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to wheat flour.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Toasted Cuban bread is used as a base for sandwiches, as a side to soups, or simply with butter and cheese. It can be cubed for salads, made into croutons, or served with avocado and tomatoes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the bread in a paper bag or cloth sack at room temperature to keep the crust crisp. For longer storage, freeze slices and toast them before eating.

content.title: About
content.content: Crisp, cherry are crunchy dried cherries processed with a special technique that preserves their natural sweetness and bright flavor. The cherries are dehydrated at low temperature, retaining most of the vitamins, minerals, and the characteristic aroma of ripe cherries.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Dried cherries retain up to 80 % of the vitamin C found in fresh fruit.
Traditional folk medicine used dried cherries to aid digestion.
Crisp, cherry contains no added sugar or preservatives.
Cherries belong to the Rosaceae family and are relatives of apples, pears, and peaches.
The crunchy texture is achieved by rapid dehydration at temperatures not exceeding 45 °C.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Cherries contain anthocyanins and polyphenols that help combat free radicals and reduce oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports heart health
items.content: Flavonoids in cherries improve vascular function and may lower LDL cholesterol levels.

items.title: Contains vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C boosts the immune system and aids collagen synthesis.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes healthy digestion and helps maintain satiety.

items.title: Supports eye health
items.content: Carotenoids and vitamin A present in cherries contribute to good vision.

items.title: Cherry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to cherries, ranging from skin rashes to more severe symptoms.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Although no sugar is added, the natural sugars in cherries may be a concern for people with diabetes.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: Cherries have moderate acidity, which can cause discomfort for those sensitive to acidic foods.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Crisp, cherry can be enjoyed as a snack, added to granola, yogurt, baked goods, salads, or used as a sweet note in sauces and desserts.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a dry, cool place in an airtight container. For long‑term storage, keep refrigerated to preserve crunch and aroma.

content.title: About
content.content: The frozen coffee drink, decaffeinated and nonfat, is a ready‑to‑serve beverage made from filtered coffee, water and a small amount of sweetener. The coffee undergoes a decaffeination process that removes almost all caffeine, and the fat is completely removed, resulting in a low‑calorie drink.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Decaffeination is usually performed by water‑based extraction or supercritical CO₂, preserving most flavor compounds.
Frozen coffee drinks are popular in hot climates where they are served as a refreshing dessert.
The nonfat version contains less than 0.5 g of fat per 100 ml, making it suitable for low‑fat diets.
Taste of decaffeinated frozen coffee is often described as smoother and slightly sweeter than regular iced coffee.
These drinks are sometimes fortified with B‑vitamins and calcium to boost nutritional value.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: With virtually no fat and modest sugar levels, the drink fits well into weight‑management plans.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Coffee is rich in polyphenols that help combat oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports hydration
items.content: The majority of the beverage is water, contributing to daily fluid intake.

items.title: No stimulant effect
items.content: Absence of caffeine makes it safe for people sensitive to stimulants.

items.title: Fortified with vitamins
items.content: Some formulations add vitamin D and calcium, beneficial for bone health.

items.title: Coffee allergy
items.content: A small number of individuals may experience allergic reactions to coffee components.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Certain versions contain added sweeteners; people with diabetes should check the label.

items.title: Cold temperature
items.content: Consuming directly from the freezer can cause discomfort for those with sensitive teeth.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the frozen coffee straight from the freezer, allowing it to soften for 2–3 minutes for a smoother texture. You can garnish with fresh berries, mint, or a sprinkle of cinnamon. It works as a snack dessert or a post‑workout refresher.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in a freezer at –18 °C or lower in the original packaging. Once opened, use within 2–3 weeks to prevent crystal formation and flavor loss. Do not leave at room temperature for more than 30 minutes.

content.title: About
content.content: Gravy is a thick sauce made from meat broth, often enriched with aromatic spices and served with roasted meat, potatoes, and vegetables. The NFS 1922 version follows a traditional recipe that includes beef broth, onion, carrot, tomato paste, spices, and a touch of cream for a smoother texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The gravy recipe originated in 19th‑century England and quickly became popular in the United States.
In 1922, NFS released its signature line of sauces, with this gravy becoming a classic staple for home meals.
Traditional gravy is made from the pan drippings left after cooking meat, giving it a deep, savory flavor.
The original recipe uses a small amount of sugar to balance the acidity of the tomatoes.
Gravy is commonly served with the classic dish “meatballs in gravy.”

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Gravy made from meat broth provides amino acids that support muscle recovery.

items.title: Source of iron
items.content: Beef broth is high in heme iron, which is more readily absorbed by the body.

items.title: Contains collagen
items.content: The broth used in the sauce supplies collagen, beneficial for joints and skin.

items.title: Low sugar content
items.content: The original recipe adds only minimal sugar, making the sauce suitable for moderate consumption.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Meat broth provides vitamins B6 and B12, important for the nervous system and blood formation.

items.title: High sodium
items.content: Gravy can be salty, so people with hypertension should watch portion sizes.

items.title: Beef allergy
items.content: Some individuals may have an allergic reaction to meat products.

items.title: Fat content
items.content: If cream is added, the sauce can be calorie‑dense and fatty.

items.title: Monosodium glutamate
items.content: Some commercial versions use flavor enhancers that may cause sensitivity in certain consumers.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve hot gravy over roasted meats, meatloaf, mashed potatoes, baked vegetables, or pasta dishes. Warm it gently on low heat, adding a splash of water or broth if it becomes too thick.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store prepared gravy in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, portion the sauce into freezer‑safe containers and freeze for up to 2 months. Reheat to a boil before serving to ensure safety.

content.title: About
content.content: Lobster is a crustacean marine product found in cold coastal waters of the Atlantic and Pacific oceans. Its meat is tender, slightly sweet, and carries a distinct sea flavor. Lobster is commonly served boiled, baked, or as a gourmet dish.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Lobsters can change the color of their shells depending on the environment and mood.
An adult lobster can live over 50 years and reach weights of more than 20 kg.
Lobsters can regenerate lost claws and legs.
The largest recorded lobster weighed over 20 kg and was caught off the coast of Canada.
Lobsters use their powerful claws not only for hunting but also for communication.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Lobster meat provides high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Compared with many seafoods, lobster contains very little fat, making it suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Source of zinc and selenium
items.content: These trace minerals support the immune system and have antioxidant properties.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Lobster supplies vitamin B12, important for nervous system function and blood formation.

items.title: Omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: A modest amount of omega‑3 contributes to heart and vascular health.

items.title: Shellfish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience severe allergic reactions to lobster.

items.title: High cholesterol content
items.content: Lobster contains cholesterol, so people with elevated cholesterol should consume it in moderation.

items.title: Toxic organs
items.content: The tomalley and hepatopancreas can accumulate toxins and are usually not eaten.

items.title: Risk of overconsumption
items.content: Because lobster is expensive, diners may eat large portions, leading to excess sodium intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Lobster is typically boiled in salted water for 8–12 minutes, then served with melted butter, lemon, or a sauce. The meat is removed from the claws and tail and can be added to salads, pastas, risottos, or served as a hot appetizer.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep live lobster on ice in the refrigerator, covered with a damp cloth, for up to 2 days. Frozen lobster should be stored at –18 °C and used within 3–4 months. Thaw frozen lobster in the refrigerator before cooking.

content.title: About
content.content: Wine is an alcoholic beverage made by fermenting grape juice or other fruit juices. Rice is a cereal grain that serves as a staple carbohydrate source in many Asian cuisines. Together they appear in traditional dishes where wine adds aroma and rice acts as a base or side.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Wine can be aged in oak barrels, imparting vanilla and spice notes.
There are over 10,000 grape varieties used for winemaking.
Rice feeds more than half of the world’s population.
More than 40,000 rice varieties exist, differing in grain shape, flavor, and cooking method.
In Japan, rice is often paired with a small amount of sake (rice wine) during ceremonies.

items.title: Antioxidants in wine
items.content: Red wine is rich in polyphenols, especially resveratrol, which may support cardiovascular health.

items.title: Energy from rice
items.content: Rice provides a quick source of complex carbohydrates, useful for athletes and active individuals.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Both wine and rice contain B1, B3, and B6 vitamins important for metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Rice supplies magnesium and phosphorus, while wine contributes modest amounts of potassium and iron.

items.title: Digestive support
items.content: Fiber in whole‑grain rice promotes healthy bowel function.

items.title: Alcohol content
items.content: Excessive wine consumption can lead to liver issues, increased disease risk, and dependence.

items.title: Sugar levels
items.content: Sweet wines contain high sugar, which may be problematic for people with diabetes.

items.title: Arsenic in rice
items.content: Certain rice strains can accumulate arsenic from soil; rinsing rice before cooking reduces this risk.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: While rice is naturally gluten‑free, some flavored wines may contain trace gluten.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve wine chilled (white) or at room temperature (red) in appropriate glasses. Cook rice in water or broth for sushi, pilaf, risotto, or as a side dish. In cooking, wine is often added to sauces, marinades, and desserts, while rice can absorb wine aromas when prepared together.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store wine in a cool, dark place on its side to keep the cork moist. Once opened, consume within 3–5 days. Keep rice in an airtight container in a cool, dry area; uncooked rice can last up to a year, while cooked rice should be refrigerated and used within 4 days.
